newsitem.title: USA: Tougher U.S. air quality standards get mixed review.
newsitem.headline: Tougher U.S. air quality standards get mixed review.

text.p: Controversial air quality standards that the Clinton administration claims would prolong the lives of 20,000 Americans every year and save billions of dollars were criticised and praised in public hearings on Tuesday.

Critics blasted the Environmental Protection Agency's proposals to tighten restrictions on allowable levels of smog-producing ozone and airborne particulates as business killers that are unnecessary because U.S. air quality has already improved.

Proponents of the new standards, which could begin to take effect in June if Congress does not object, said cleaner air would allay the rising incidence of crippling respiratory ailments such as asthma.

EPA officials heard from a broad array of health care advocates, industry representatives, government officials and other interested parties as the agency began two days of public hearings in Chicago, Boston and Salt Lake City.

"We believe the EPA is recklessly rushing forward while ignoring its own scientific board's analysis," David Saykuta, executive director of the Illinois Petroleum Council, told the Chicago panel. "This will bring a painfully high cost ... The proposed rules ignore the spectacular progress made in cleaning the air."

He said the stricter standards would raise prices to consumers, stifle job growth and create "lifestyle police" that would dictate whether people could use charcoal grills, snowblowers, lawn mowers or drive to work alone.
Mary Nichols, EPA assistant administrator for air quality who was chairing the Chicago hearing, later told reporters the alarms raised by business and industry were often overblown.
"Some of the threats of immediate economic harm are scare tactics," Nichols said.
The EPA would require states and cities to lower the levels of the pollutants significantly over the next decade, with the threat of losing federal funds to states that fail to comply.

The agency predicted direct "benefits" in terms of lower mortality rates and hospital costs of as much as $144 billion a year beginning in 2007, while "costs" of implementing the pollution controls could reach only $10 billion.

Currently, 74 million people live in areas that violate current standards for ozone pollution, and the new stricter levels would put 122 million people in non-complying areas. For particulates such as dust and soot that can be microscopic in size, the number of people living in areas violating federal standards would rise to 74 million from 29 million.
The standards for ground-level ozone and particulates have not changed since 1979 and 1987, respectively.
Nichols said the agency needed to adjust how it assesses efforts to improve air quality, including finding ways to account for pollution generated elsewhere that drifts downwind.
Joan Benoit Samuelson, an Olympic marathon winner, said she feels the effects of air pollution and has seen it in others.

"I have felt the painful and somewhat serious effects of increased ozone levels and particulate matter in my chest and lungs as I have trained," said Samuelson, who travelled from her home in Freeport, Maine to testify at the Boston hearing. "As I continue to run in competitive events, I see more and more athletes of all abilities and ages depending on inhalers to combat environmentally-induced asthma. Elite athletes are beginning to choose events based on air quality."
Kyle Damitz, an 8-year-old asthma sufferer, said that he suffered terribly during summer days when ozone levels rose.
"I cannot play outside. If you pass the clean air laws, I will be able to play," he testified at the Chicago hearing.
The American Lung Association, which strongly supports the stricter standards, has blamed air pollution for 60,000 deaths annually in the United States.

Oil refiners, boat manufacturers, truckers and automakers testified against the standards, claiming they placed too large a burden on business and urged delays and more careful study. "Pollution will continue to decline when additional controls required by the (1990) Clean Air Act are implemented and given a chance to work," said James Brett of the New England Council, which represents more than 250 businesses.
